content:
I want to share some thoughts on AI and Lean that I haven’t seen posted yet, but which I think are important to the discussion.

Mathematics was something I have long been interested in but felt locked out of because when I try to express my ideas I sound like I can't tie my shoelaces. For some reason AI makes it easier for me to overcome my communication difficulties and write down what’s in my head. The combination with Lean has turned out to be unusually powerful: AI makes my thoughts communicable and Lean prevents communicability from masquerading as correctness. And it is more than just a transcription machine: AI has served as a valuable collaborator in challenging and critically reviewing my ideas which others often find idiosyncratic or difficult to engage with. It has given me access to a part of myself that I previously felt locked out of.

Perhaps this is why I also feel very critical toward Anthropic and OpenAI at this time for making big plays with FLT and NS and for offering grants at their discretion. While Lean and AI have opened a door which I am intensely grateful for, I am deeply concerned by the possibility that AI companies will serve as the gatekeepers. The tragedy would be for this liberating technology to remain a revocable favor granted by a few corporations, who can inspect everyone who walks through the door and who receives subsidized admission.

I don’t have an answer to where I think things should go from here. Given the personal impact and the simple observation that it is too powerful to simply sweep under the rug, I think whatever becomes the blessed path should include AI in some capacity. But I also don’t want to live in a world where mathematical advances are dominated by corporate sponsorship, a direction we seem to be heading.

I feel cautious about phrasing any path as a "blessed path". I think that even given the enormous pressure those companies have been making and the objective capacity of those models, we don't really understand how it's going to be valued by different people and what good this increase in productivity serves in the end. So I would rather have a world that encourages diverse use of AI (including no use at all, if that makes sense for the person) instead of accepting a discourse that academia should be making use of a tool in a certain way.

felt locked out of because when I try to express my ideas I sound like I can't tie my shoelaces

The reality is that even with "AI", we are still locked out of the areas we didn't learn the old fashioned way, and the more pressing concern is not that some corporations might lock us out of some "intellegence" we rely on thus deem deserved, but that we have given up engaging with the subject the hard way.

All the learning, practices, expressions with LLMs/agents as proxies are not ours. The empowering is a delusion. We may have things explained to us by LLMs using expressions we can understand, but we can never be certain about what are lost or twisted in the process, and we have gained no real understading thus can't exercise any real judgement beyond what we have already mastered in the old fashioned way.

On the other hand, anything produced by LLMs could go wrong in the worst way we can't even imagine without such expertise (e.g. changing a Lean statement while keeping its docstring faithful to the informal math, and trusting the docstring in an adversarial review instead of verifying the Lean statement; unable to attribute properly because some souces available publicly had become part of the training corpus, causing severe plagiarism risks for any research conducted with LLM assistance, even in good faith).

In the end, we might realize that "attention is all we get" from LLMs. Fixing LaTeX or Lean setup issues saves our attention bandwidth for the math subject; literature search leads us to notice their existence then we should read them first-hand; adversarial reviews may help or worsen our attention distribution depending on whether it floods us with less important issues or leads us to what matters, or even silently accepts some serious issues (LLMs might notice them in thinking process, but deemed them non-issue due to some "honest" disclaimer theater); agent exploration and verification also can't reliably rule out or confirm a route or an hypotheses without careful inspection. All the unlocking are still done by our own intelligence.

When we are engaging with "AI", we are not reaching the actual depth of our civilization it is trained on, we are simply looking at a mirror at our own depth. Using "AI" is like driving a car that has ever changing behavior and dashboards without windows for a first-hand observation, we are used to certain behaviors or dashboard signals, but they can secrectly change underneath, and we can't realize that we are already far off road.

I think you might be reading into my point a little too much @Utensil Song, I just meant that I struggle with the language process of turning math into words and LLMs work as serviceable translators. I suspect non native english speakers benefit similarly for things like writing english documents.

I suspect non native english speakers benefit similarly for things like writing english documents.

This is a good example. My personal experience is that interacting with LLMs is making my language instincts worse and I have to rely on what I have learned before any interaction with LLMs to calibrate. It would be more obvious when the defects of LLM responses are in my native language, but as for English, LLM outputs I have to work with only disoriented me from being able to tell what is more native, e.g. I may take Claudish as English. For languages that I don't know well, e.g. I can barely read French, but I couldn't trust any French I learned from interaction with LLMs, because I haven't developed any language instincts in French to tell the difference. Same applies to Lean and math.

Same applies to math or any professional knowledge, but worse, because in there it may be easier to tap into the void of the semantics and make huge mistakes. Anything generated by LLMs originally are either based on corpus, interpolated or extrapolated, and if we still haven't lost the touch we can easily see which is the case. But due to the inference time scaling law and heavy post-training, these are now deeply buried into reasoning chains that are also Intentional hidden, and worse, has a deeper cause in the synthetic corpus and agent traces.

This can be better examined by areas we are familiar with, by verifiable output. Before learning anything with LLMs, we should validate the limits with the areas we know well; and when we start to learn anything new with them, we should try to reduce the judgment back to the areas we know well, so we can have at least some judgement. The process has exhausted me to the point that I realized any convenience gained by using LLMs to learn, has to be compensated by more work with my already disoriented mind. Working with agents at scale, has also significantly increased the risk exposure, and even increase the verification work to a prohibitable cost.

To combat the situation, it seems to me that "AI companies serving as the gatekeepers" or "doing evil" is not the issue here, it is that what kind of intellegence should we artificially create to work with.
